intro: Freemasons are one of the best-known fraternities in the world. Their square and compasses sign hangs on lodge buildings in towns across America, including many in Illinois. People also tell many stories about them. Some say Masons built the pyramids. Some say they planned the American Revolution or hid symbols on the dollar bill. Which stories are true?

In this unit you will follow the Masons from the building sites of medieval England and Scotland to the founding of the United States. You will read a rulebook in rhyme from about 1390, the oldest lodge minute from 1599, and one famous line in a scholar's diary. Then you will meet founders who were Masons and founders who were not, and trace the eye on the dollar back to 1776.

By the end, you will be able to sort a claim into three kinds: documented, disputed or unsupported. You will be able to name the record that proves a fact, notice when a story is a legend, and write a fair answer that gives both sides their due.
bigQuestion: How did working stonemasons become the Freemasons, and how can records help us sort true stories about them from legends?

timeline.t: The Regius Poem, the oldest known rulebook for masons, is written in England.
Aitchison's Haven lodge in Scotland writes the oldest surviving lodge minute.
Elias Ashmole writes in his diary that he was made a Free Mason at Warrington.
Traditional date of the first Grand Lodge in London; some historians argue for 1721.
James Anderson publishes The Constitutions of the Free-Masons.
Pope Clement XII issues the first papal ban on Freemasonry.
George Washington, age 20, joins the lodge at Fredericksburg, Virginia.
The first Great Seal committee proposes the Eye of Providence in a triangle.
Congress adopts the Great Seal, with the unfinished pyramid on the back.
Washington helps lay the U.S. Capitol cornerstone in a Masonic ceremony.
John Adams writes that he was never a Mason; Washington writes that he rarely attends a lodge.
The eye and pyramid of the Great Seal are first printed on the one-dollar bill.

test.why: The Regius Poem, about 1390, is the oldest known of the Old Charges.

test.q: Why did Scottish lodges begin keeping minutes in 1599?

test.why: The Schaw Statutes of 1598 and 1599 told lodges to keep written records.

test.q: The King Athelstan story in the Regius Poem is best described as what?
test.why: No record shows Athelstan met the masons, so historians treat the story as a legend.

test.q: What does Ashmole's 1646 diary entry prove?
choices: Ashmole was Grand Master of England
A gentleman who was not a builder joined a lodge in England
test.why: Ashmole, a scholar, recorded that he was made a Free Mason at Warrington in 1646.

test.why: Operative masons built for a living; speculative members did not build and used tools as symbols.

test.q: Why is the Grand Lodge's founding date disputed?

No lodges existed in London until 1800
Ashmole wrote that it began in 1646
The Grand Lodge was founded in Scotland

It welcomed men of different churches
It made Masonry a new religion

Secret oaths and mixing men of all religions
Voting in elections and paying taxes

test.why: The Fredericksburg lodge ledger records Washington joining on 4 November 1752.

He is not known to have been a Mason

write.prompt: A classmate says: "The Freemasons designed the United States, and the dollar bill proves it." Is this claim documented, disputed or unsupported? Use at least three facts or sources from this unit to explain your answer.
tips: Name each source you use, such as the 1776 committee report or Adams's 1798 letter.
Split the claim into parts: who designed the seal, who put it on the dollar, and which founders were Masons.
Give the claim its fair due: say which parts have some truth.
Use unit words like primary source, paper trail and absence of evidence.
End with a clear conclusion in one or two sentences.

title: From Stonemasons to Freemasons

chapters.title: Guilds, Lodges and the First Grand Lodge
chapters.bigQuestion: How did groups of working stonemasons turn into a club of gentlemen, and how do we know?

story.title: One Line in a Diary
story.kicker: In 1646, a scholar writes one short sentence in his diary, and historians are still talking about it.
paragraphs: It is October 1646 in the north of England. The country is at war with itself. The king's army and the army of Parliament have been fighting for four years. Elias Ashmole is on the losing side. He is a scholar and a royalist officer who loves old books, the stars and collecting curious objects.

On the 16th of October, Ashmole is in the town of Warrington in Lancashire. That day he writes a short note in his diary. He says he was made a Free Mason at Warrington, together with a relative, Colonel Henry Mainwaring. Then he lists the names of the men who were there.

Ashmole is not a builder. He has never cut a block of stone for money. So why would a lodge of masons welcome him? What did it mean to be "made a Free Mason" in 1646? The diary does not say. Ashmole mentions Masonry only once more, many years later.

Today historians treat that one line as proof of something important. A gentleman joined a lodge in England in 1646, and he wrote it down himself. But they still argue about what kind of lodge it was and what happened in that room. One sentence can open a door to the past. It can also leave the door only half open.
story.think: Why might a single sentence in a diary be stronger evidence than a long story written a hundred years later?

lessons.title: Masons and Their Lodges
lessons.mainIdea: Medieval masons were skilled stone workers, and their lodge was first a workshop at the building site.
reading: Picture a cathedral being built in England about 700 years ago. Carts bring blocks of stone. Men cut, shape and lift each block by hand. The work can take fifty years or more. Some workers spend their whole lives on one building.

These workers were *masons*, people who build with stone. The most skilled ones carved fine stone for windows, arches and statues. They moved from job to job, wherever a church, castle or bridge was being built.

At the building site, the masons had a shed or hut called a *lodge*. It was a place to work out of the rain, keep tools, eat and rest. Over time, the word lodge also came to mean the group of masons who worked there together.

Where does the name "freemason" come from? Historians give more than one answer. One idea links it to "freestone," a soft, fine stone that could be carved. Another links it to workers who were free to travel. The honest answer is that we are not certain.

words.d: a skilled worker who builds with stone
first a workshop hut at a building site; later, the group of masons who met there

look.title: A Day at the Building Site
look.text: Rain is falling on a half-built cathedral. The stone cutters carry their chisels and mallets into a wooden hut beside the wall. Inside, one mason traces the curve of a window on a board. Two apprentices sweep up stone dust. An older mason checks a block with a metal square.
look.prompt: Name two jobs the lodge hut did for these workers. Why would the name of the hut come to mean the group of people inside it?

check.q: In the Middle Ages, what was a mason's lodge at first?
choices: A workshop hut at the building site
A bank that paid the workers
A school in a big city
check.why: The reading says the lodge was a shed or hut at the site where masons worked, kept tools and rested.

check.q: What did the most skilled masons carve?
choices: Fine stone for windows, arches and statues
check.why: The reading says the most skilled masons carved fine stone for windows, arches and statues.

check.q: What does the reading say about where the word freemason comes from?
choices: A king invented the word in 1390
It comes from a word for secret
It was first used in America
Historians give more than one answer and are not certain
check.why: The reading gives two ideas, freestone and free to travel, and says we are not certain.

lessons.title: The Regius Poem
lessons.mainIdea: The Regius Poem, written about 1390, is the oldest known text of rules for masons.
reading: In the British Library in London sits a small book made of *vellum*, a writing material made from animal skin. It is only a few inches tall. Inside is a long poem in Middle English, the English of about 1390. Scholars call it the Regius Poem.

The poem is a rulebook in rhyme. It tells masons to do honest work and take fair pay. It tells a master to treat apprentices well. It even gives advice on good manners at church and at the table. It sounds a lot like a code of conduct for a workplace today.

For centuries, the little book sat in the royal library. Its catalogue called it a poem about moral duties. In 1838 and 1839 a young scholar, James Halliwell, read it closely. He saw that it was about the masons' craft. He published it in 1840. Halliwell was not a Mason himself.

Texts like this one are called the *Old Charges*. A charge is a duty or an instruction. The Regius Poem is the oldest known Old Charge. Its date comes from the handwriting and the language, so scholars say "about 1390."

words.d: a fine writing material made from animal skin, used for books before paper was common
old texts that gave masons their rules and told legends about the craft

look.title: Rules for a Good Mason
look.text: The poem tells the master to pay his workers fairly and not to take a job he cannot finish. It tells masons to be true to one another and to keep their master's business private. It asks them to behave well in church and to have good manners at meals.
look.cite: The Regius Poem (Halliwell Manuscript), about 1390, British Library, Royal MS 17 A I (summary in modern English)
look.prompt: Which of these rules would still make sense at a job today? Which one surprises you?

check.q: About when was the Regius Poem written?
check.why: Scholars date the Regius Poem to about 1390 from its handwriting and language.

check.q: What kind of text is the Regius Poem?
choices: A rulebook for masons written in rhyme
A newspaper story about a war
check.why: The reading calls it a rulebook in rhyme that gives masons their duties.

check.q: Who noticed in 1838 and 1839 that the poem was about masons?
choices: Elias Ashmole, who wrote a diary
James Halliwell, a scholar who was not a Mason
check.why: The reading says James Halliwell saw what the poem was about and published it in 1840.

lessons.title: Legends the Masons Told
lessons.mainIdea: The Old Charges mix real rules with legends, and a careful reader keeps the two apart.
reading: The Old Charges do more than list rules. They also tell a history of the craft. The Regius Poem says an old English king, Athelstan, gathered the masons and gave them their articles and points, a set of rules. Athelstan was a real king in the 900s.

A second old text, the Cooke Manuscript, was written about 1450. It tells an even bigger story. It links masonry to geometry, to the Greek thinker Euclid and to the building of King Solomon's temple in Jerusalem. These stories made the craft sound very old and very noble.

Historians call these stories a *legend*, a story handed down that may hold some truth but cannot be proved. No record shows that Athelstan met the masons. The Solomon story is a way of honoring the craft, not a record of it.

Many groups tell origin stories like this. Towns, schools and families do it too. The stories tell us what a group was proud of. They are worth reading as legends. They are not the same as *evidence*.

words.d: a story handed down over time that may hold some truth but cannot be proved
records, objects or facts that show whether something really happened

look.title: Two Kinds of Old Writing
look.text: Text A, about 1450: the craft of masonry began with geometry, and great kings of old honored the masons who built their temples. Text B, 1599: on this day in the lodge, a named man was made a fellow of the craft, and his name is written in the book.
look.prompt: Which text is a legend, and which is a record? What clues helped you decide?

check.q: Which king does the Regius Poem say gave masons their rules?
check.why: The reading says the Regius Poem tells of King Athelstan, a real king of the 900s, giving the masons rules.

check.q: What does the Cooke Manuscript link masonry to?
check.why: The reading says the Cooke Manuscript, about 1450, links masonry to geometry, Euclid and Solomon's temple.

check.q: Why do historians call the Athelstan story a legend?
choices: No record shows that Athelstan met the masons
Athelstan was never a real king
check.why: The reading says Athelstan was real, but no record shows he met the masons, so the story is a legend.

lessons.title: William Schaw's Rules
lessons.mainIdea: In 1598 and 1599, the king's builder in Scotland gave lodges written rules and told them to keep records.
reading: William Schaw was the Master of Works for King James VI of Scotland. That meant he was in charge of the king's buildings. On 28 December 1598 he signed a set of rules for the masons of Scotland. A second set followed on 28 December 1599.

Historians call them the Schaw *Statutes*. A statute is a written rule or law. Schaw's rules covered safety at work, fines for bad work and how to train apprentices. An apprentice is a young worker learning a trade from a master.

One rule changed history. Schaw told the lodges to keep written records of their meetings. Because of that order, some Scottish lodges began to write things down. Those papers are the oldest lodge records in the world.
The original of the first statutes is kept by the Lodge of Edinburgh, known as Mary's Chapel. That lodge still meets today. So a rulebook from the 1590s still belongs to the group it was written for.

words.d: a written rule or law made by someone in charge
a young worker who learns a trade by working for a skilled master

look.title: Rules for a Class Workshop
look.text: Imagine your class is building a big model bridge. You write four rules. Wear safety glasses. Redo any piece that is not straight. Older students help the new ones. Write down what we did at the end of each day.
look.prompt: Which of your rules is most like Schaw's order to keep records? Why would that rule help historians hundreds of years later?

check.q: What job did William Schaw have?
choices: Master of Works for King James VI
check.why: The reading says Schaw was Master of Works, in charge of the king's buildings, for James VI of Scotland.

check.q: Which of Schaw's rules led to the oldest lodge records?
choices: Lodges must build a church each year
Lodges must keep written records of meetings
check.why: The reading says Schaw told lodges to write down their meetings, and those papers are the oldest lodge records.

check.q: What is an apprentice?
choices: A young worker learning a trade from a master
check.why: The reading defines an apprentice as a young worker learning a trade from a master.

lessons.title: The Oldest Lodge Minute
lessons.mainIdea: The oldest surviving lodge minute, from January 1599, records a real man joining the craft.
reading: A *minute* is a written note of what happened at a meeting. Clubs and school boards still keep minutes today. The oldest lodge minute that survives comes from a lodge called Aitchison's Haven, near Edinburgh in Scotland.

It is dated 9 January 1599. On that day, the lodge recorded that a man named Robert Widderspone was made a Fellow of Craft. A Fellow of Craft was a fully trained mason, one step above an apprentice. The page is now kept by the Grand Lodge of Scotland.

There is a small puzzle in the date. The minute itself says 1598. In Scotland back then, the new year began on 25 March, not 1 January. So January came near the end of the year 1598. By our calendar, it was January 1599.

A few months later, on 31 July 1599, the Lodge of Edinburgh began its own minutes. Aitchison's Haven closed in 1852. The Lodge of Edinburgh still meets. So its records are the oldest of any lodge that still exists.

words.d: a written record of what happened at a meeting
a fully trained mason, one step above an apprentice

look.title: The Oldest Mason Papers
look.cite: British Library catalogue; David Stevenson, The Origins of Freemasonry, Cambridge University Press, 1988
look.prompt: How many years passed between the Regius Poem and the oldest lodge minute? Which two papers are closest together in time?

check.q: What is a minute in a lodge or club?
choices: A tiny piece of carved stone
A written record of what happened at a meeting
check.why: The reading defines a minute as a written note of what happened at a meeting.

check.q: Why does the Aitchison's Haven minute say 1598 when we call it 1599?
choices: In Scotland then, the new year began on 25 March
The writer made a spelling mistake
check.why: The reading explains that the Scottish year began on 25 March, so January still counted as 1598.

check.q: Which lodge has the oldest records of any lodge that still meets?
check.why: Aitchison's Haven closed in 1852, but the Lodge of Edinburgh, with minutes from July 1599, still meets.

lessons.title: The Mason Word and the Memory Test
lessons.mainIdea: Scottish masons used a secret word and memory tests to prove that a worker was truly trained.
reading: Imagine a mason walking to a job in a town where no one knows him. He says he trained for years. How can the other masons be sure? In Scotland, a trained mason could prove it with the *Mason Word*, a secret word and sign known only to trained masons.

A paper from 1696, now called the Edinburgh Register House Manuscript, shows how this worked. It lists questions masons asked a stranger who claimed to have the Mason Word. It is the oldest known written set of these questions.

Schaw's second statutes, from December 1599, add another clue. They told the lodge at Kilwinning to test every fellow and apprentice on the "art of memory." Masons had to remember a lot without writing it down.

Historian David Stevenson links this rule to the memory arts of the time. Scholars then used a *memory palace*, picturing a building and placing each fact in a room. Not every historian agrees on how far to take this link. But the rule shows that memory mattered in the lodge.

words.d: a secret word and sign that Scottish masons used to prove they were trained
a way to remember by picturing a building and placing each fact in a room

look.title: A Test of Memory, 1599
look.text: The warden of the lodge at Kilwinning is to test every fellow of the craft and every apprentice on the art of memory, each according to his level of training.
look.cite: Second Schaw Statutes, 28 December 1599, as transcribed in The Square magazine (modern English paraphrase)
look.prompt: Why would a trade with few written papers care so much about memory?

check.q: What was the Mason Word used for?
choices: To prove that a mason was truly trained
check.why: The reading says a trained mason could prove his training with the Mason Word.

check.q: What does the 1696 Edinburgh Register House Manuscript contain?
choices: Questions masons asked a stranger who claimed the Mason Word
check.why: The reading says it lists questions masons asked a stranger and is the oldest known written set of them.

check.q: What did the 1599 statutes tell the Kilwinning lodge to test?
check.why: The reading says Schaw's second statutes told Kilwinning to test every fellow and apprentice on the art of memory.

lessons.title: Ashmole's Diary Line
lessons.mainIdea: Elias Ashmole's diary entry of 16 October 1646 is the earliest clear English record of a gentleman joining a lodge.
reading: Elias Ashmole lived from 1617 to 1692. He studied law, history, the stars and old books. He collected rare objects. Later he gave his collection to Oxford University. It became the Ashmolean Museum, one of the oldest public museums in the world.

Ashmole kept a diary. On 16 October 1646 he wrote that he was made a Free Mason at Warrington in Lancashire. He named his relative Colonel Henry Mainwaring and listed the other men who were there. A diary written on the day is a *primary source*, a record made by someone who was there.

Why does this line matter? Ashmole was not a stonemason. He was a gentleman scholar. His note is the earliest clear record in England of a man like him joining a lodge. Before this, English records of lodges are very thin.

The line also leaves questions. Were the other men in the room working masons, or gentlemen too? What happened in the ceremony? Historians still debate these questions. The diary proves that Ashmole joined. It does not explain everything about what joining meant.

words.d: a record made at the time by someone who was there, such as a diary or letter
in older times, a man of good family or wealth who did not work with his hands for a living

look.title: Ashmole's Diary, 1646
look.text: Ashmole writes that on this day he was made a Free Mason at Warrington in Lancashire, together with Colonel Henry Mainwaring of Cheshire. He then lists by name the men who were in the lodge, including a warden named Richard Penket.
look.cite: Elias Ashmole, diary entry, 16 October 1646, as reprinted in The Masonic Magazine, 1881; standard edition by C. H. Josten, Oxford, 1966
look.prompt: What does this entry prove for sure? What questions does it leave open?

check.q: What did Elias Ashmole's collection later become?
check.why: The reading says Ashmole gave his collection to Oxford University and it became the Ashmolean Museum.

check.q: Why do historians treat Ashmole's diary as a primary source?
choices: A Masonic lodge wrote it in 1900
He wrote it at the time about his own life
It was carved on a cathedral
It was printed as a legend
check.why: A primary source is a record made at the time by someone who was there, like Ashmole's own diary.

check.q: What does the diary NOT tell us?
check.why: The reading says the diary proves he joined at Warrington in 1646, but not what happened in the ceremony.

lessons.title: Working Masons and Thinking Masons
lessons.mainIdea: Over the 1600s, men who never cut stone joined lodges, and the tools of building became symbols for lessons about life.
reading: Ashmole was not the only gentleman to join. During the 1600s, lawyers, doctors, landowners and scholars joined lodges in Scotland and England. Some lodges came to have more gentlemen than working masons.

Historians use two words for this change. *Operative* masons were working builders who cut and set stone for a living. *Speculative* masons were members who did not build. Speculative comes from a Latin word about looking and thinking.

Speculative masons used building tools as symbols. A square, used to check a right angle, came to stand for fair and honest dealing. That is where the phrase "on the square" comes from. A pair of compasses, used to draw circles, came to stand for keeping one's actions within limits.

How did this change happen? The Scottish records show lodges slowly taking in gentlemen. The English records are thinner. Some historians see one long, slow growth. Others see new clubs borrowing an old craft's name and legends. The question is still open.

words.d: describes working masons who built with stone for a living
describes lodge members who did not build but used masons' tools as symbols
an object or picture that stands for an idea

look.title: From Tool to Symbol
look.text: A builder uses a square to check that each corner of a stone is exactly true. A lodge member holds up the same tool and says: this reminds us to deal fairly and honestly with every person. The tool has not changed. What it stands for has.
look.prompt: Pick a tool from your own classroom. What idea could it stand for? Explain your choice.

check.q: What is an operative mason?
choices: A working builder who cuts and sets stone
A judge in a lodge trial
check.why: The reading says operative masons were working builders who cut and set stone for a living.

check.q: In speculative masonry, what did the square come to stand for?
check.why: The reading says the square came to stand for fair and honest dealing, which gave us the phrase on the square.

check.q: What do historians still debate about this change?
choices: Whether stone was used in cathedrals
Whether the square is a building tool
Whether it was slow growth or new clubs borrowing an old name
check.why: The reading says some see one long, slow growth and others see new clubs borrowing the craft's name.

lessons.title: A Grand Lodge in London
lessons.mainIdea: A Grand Lodge formed in London, traditionally in 1717, though some historians argue it really began about 1721.
reading: By the early 1700s, several lodges of gentlemen met in London taverns. At some point, a few of them joined together under one leader. They formed a *Grand Lodge*, a governing body over many lodges. Its leader was called the Grand Master.

The traditional story says four London lodges met on 24 June 1717 at a tavern called the Goose and Gridiron. There they formed the Grand Lodge. Grand Lodges around the world celebrated its 300th birthday in 2017.

But where does the 1717 story come from? Almost all of it comes from one book, the second edition of James Anderson's Constitutions, printed in 1738. That was more than twenty years after the event. No record from 1717 itself has been found.

In 2017, historians Andrew Prescott and Susan Mitchell Sommers argued that the Grand Lodge really began around 1721. That year the Duke of Montagu, a famous nobleman, became Grand Master. Other historians still defend 1717. This is a *disputed* question, and both sides point to evidence.

words.d: a governing body that leads many lodges in one area
argued about by experts, with no final answer yet

look.title: Dates in the Grand Lodge Debate
rows: Duke of Montagu becomes Grand Master
Anderson's second edition tells the 1717 story
look.cite: Andrew Prescott and Susan Mitchell Sommers, Searching for the Apple Tree, 2017
look.prompt: How many years after 1717 was the 1717 story first printed? Why might that gap make a historian cautious?

check.q: What is the traditional founding date of the Grand Lodge in London?
check.why: The traditional story says four lodges met on 24 June 1717 at the Goose and Gridiron tavern.

check.q: Why do some historians doubt the 1717 date?
choices: The Goose and Gridiron was in Scotland
The story was first printed in 1738, with no record from 1717
check.why: The reading says the 1717 story comes from Anderson's 1738 edition, and no record from 1717 has been found.

check.q: What happened in 1721, according to Prescott and Sommers?
choices: The Duke of Montagu became Grand Master
The first lodge minute was written
check.why: Prescott and Sommers argue the Grand Lodge really began about 1721, when the Duke of Montagu became Grand Master.

lessons.title: Anderson's Constitutions
lessons.mainIdea: Anderson's Constitutions of 1723 gave the new Grand Lodge a rulebook and opened lodges to men of different churches.
reading: In 1723 a Scottish minister in London, James Anderson, published The Constitutions of the Free-Masons. A *constitution* is a set of basic rules for a group. This one gave the Grand Lodge its rules and a long, legend-filled history of the craft.

The first charge was about God and religion. It said a Mason must obey the moral law. Then it did something new. It asked Masons to hold only the religion in which all men agree, and to keep their own opinions to themselves. In 1723, most clubs and governments tied membership to one church.

Other rules told members not to argue about politics or religion in the lodge. The lodge was meant to be a calm place where men who disagreed outside could meet as friends. In a time of bitter quarrels over church and king, that was a new idea.

The book traveled far. Lodges in many places used it as their guide. In 1734, Benjamin Franklin reprinted it in Philadelphia. It was the first Masonic book printed in America. A London rulebook now had readers across the ocean.

words.d: a written set of basic rules for a group or a country
a duty or instruction given to members of a group

look.title: The First Charge, 1723
look.text: A Mason is bound to obey the moral law. If he truly understands the craft, he will never be a person without faith or without morals. Masons are asked to keep to the religion that all men agree on, and to keep their own particular opinions to themselves.
look.cite: James Anderson, The Constitutions of the Free-Masons, London, 1723, first charge (modern English paraphrase)
look.prompt: Why might this rule have made it easier for men from different churches to meet as friends?

check.q: Who published The Constitutions of the Free-Masons in 1723?
check.why: The reading says James Anderson, a Scottish minister in London, published the Constitutions in 1723.

check.q: What was new about the first charge on religion?
choices: It required every Mason to be Catholic
It banned all prayer in lodges
It opened lodges to men of different churches
It made the Grand Master a priest
check.why: The reading says it asked Masons to hold only the religion all men agree in, which opened lodges to men of different churches.

check.q: Who reprinted the Constitutions in Philadelphia in 1734?
check.why: The reading says Franklin reprinted it in 1734, the first Masonic book printed in America.

lessons.title: Degrees, Symbols and Charity
lessons.mainIdea: Lodges taught members through steps called degrees, used building symbols, and helped members in need.
reading: A new member moved through steps called *degrees*. By about 1730 there were three: Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason. The names came from the old building trade. Each degree had its own ceremony.

A *ritual* is a ceremony done the same way each time. Masonic rituals used short plays, questions and answers, and symbols. The legends inside them were still changing. A paper from 1726, the Graham Manuscript, tells a story about Noah's sons, not the story later Masons used.

Members promised to keep the rituals private. Outsiders were curious. In 1730, a writer named Samuel Prichard printed Masonry Dissected, which claimed to reveal all three degrees. It sold very well. Books like it are called exposés.

Lodges were also about *charity*, giving help to people in need. Lodges collected money to help members who fell on hard times and the families of members who died. Members saw this as one of the main duties of a Mason.

words.d: one of the steps or levels a member passes through in a lodge
a ceremony done the same way each time
help, often money, given to people in need

look.title: Why Keep a Ceremony Private?
look.text: A sports team has a secret cheer that only players learn. A family has a birthday tradition it does not post online. A lodge asks new members to promise to keep its ceremonies private. These are safe secrets. They are about belonging, not about hiding harm.
look.prompt: Why do groups like private traditions? How is a safe secret different from a secret that hides someone getting hurt?

check.q: What were the three degrees by about 1730?
choices: Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason
check.why: The reading names the three degrees: Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason.

check.q: What did Samuel Prichard's Masonry Dissected (1730) claim to do?
choices: Reveal all three degrees to the public
check.why: The reading says Prichard's book claimed to reveal all three degrees and sold very well.

check.q: What does the Graham Manuscript of 1726 show?
check.why: The reading says the Graham Manuscript tells a story about Noah's sons, not the later story, so the legends were still changing.

lessons.title: The Pope's Ban of 1738
lessons.mainIdea: In 1738 Pope Clement XII banned Catholics from joining the Masons, mainly because of their secret oaths and mixing of religions.
reading: Freemasonry spread fast across Europe in the 1720s and 1730s. Lodges opened in France, Italy and other Catholic countries. Church leaders grew worried about groups that met in private.

On 28 April 1738, Pope Clement XII issued a *papal bull*, an official letter from the pope, called In eminenti. It was the first time the Catholic Church condemned Freemasonry. Catholics who joined a lodge faced *excommunication*, being cut off from the Church's sacraments.

The bull gave two main reasons. Masons swore oaths of secrecy, so the Church could not know what they did. And lodges mixed men of all religions as equals, which the Church saw as a danger to faith. Some historians also point to the politics of the time, when lodges were linked to rival kings. They disagree about how much that mattered.

Members saw things differently. To them, the lodge was a place of friendship and moral teaching, open to good men of any faith. Both views help explain the long tension between the Church and the lodges.

words.d: an official letter or order from the pope
being cut off by the Catholic Church from its sacraments and full membership
a serious promise, often made in a ceremony

look.title: Two Views of the Same Lodge
look.text: View A, a Church leader in 1738: these men swear secret oaths, and they treat all religions as equal. We cannot know what they teach. View B, a lodge member: we meet as friends, we help widows, and we never argue about religion. Good men of any faith are welcome.
look.prompt: What does each side worry about or value? Can both descriptions be partly true?

choices: Secret oaths and mixing men of all religions

chapters.title: Freemasons and the American Founding
chapters.bigQuestion: Which founders were really Masons, and how can the paper trail test a popular claim?

story.title: The Eye on the Dollar
story.kicker: A student holds up a one-dollar bill and asks a question that takes the whole class back to 1776.
paragraphs: It is a gray Tuesday in a middle school classroom. The lesson is about the American Revolution. Maya raises her hand. She is holding a one-dollar bill she found in her backpack. She turns it over and points to the back.

"Who put that eye on top of the pyramid?" she asks. "My cousin says the Freemasons did. He says they secretly designed the whole country." A few students lean in. The eye does look mysterious. It floats inside a glowing triangle above a pyramid with no top.

Her teacher smiles. "That is a great question," he says. "Lots of people have heard that story. So let's test it. Who designed that picture? When? Were they Masons? What papers do we have from the time?" He writes three words on the board: Who. When. Proof.

Over the next few days, the class follows a trail of old papers. There is a committee report from 1776. There is a vote in Congress from 1782. There are letters written by two founders in 1798. And there is a decision about the dollar made in 1935. Each paper adds a piece. By the end, Maya can answer her own question, with evidence.
story.think: Before you read the chapter, what would you need to see to believe that Masons designed the eye on the dollar?

lessons.title: Franklin, Printer and Mason
lessons.mainIdea: Benjamin Franklin joined a Philadelphia lodge in 1731 and became a leading Mason and a printer of Masonic books.
reading: In 1730, Benjamin Franklin was a young printer in Philadelphia. He owned a newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette. In December 1730 his paper reported that several lodges of Freemasons had been set up in the colony. People were curious and guessing about them. Franklin's tone was a bit teasing.

A few months later, Franklin joined one of those lodges himself. He became a member of St. John's Lodge in Philadelphia in 1731. By 1734 he was *Grand Master* of the Masons of Pennsylvania, the leader of all the lodges there.

That same year, Franklin used his press to reprint Anderson's Constitutions. It was the first Masonic book printed in America. Later, while he lived in France, Franklin belonged to a famous Paris lodge called the Nine Sisters.
Franklin's story shows how a *fraternity*, a brotherhood club, could spread through print. A rulebook from London crossed the ocean and was sold in Philadelphia by a printer who was also a member.

words.d: the elected leader of all the lodges in one area
a club or brotherhood of men who share rules and goals

look.title: From Joke to Member
look.text: December 1730: Franklin's newspaper tells readers that people have been busy guessing about the new lodges in the colony. 1731: Franklin joins St. John's Lodge. 1734: Franklin is Grand Master of Pennsylvania and prints the Masons' rulebook.
look.prompt: How did Franklin's view of the lodges seem to change in four years? What might explain the change?

check.why: The reading says Franklin reprinted Anderson's Constitutions in 1734, the first Masonic book printed in America.

lessons.title: Young Washington Joins
lessons.mainIdea: George Washington joined a lodge in Fredericksburg, Virginia, in 1752, when he was 20 years old.
reading: On 4 November 1752, a lodge in Fredericksburg, Virginia, wrote a short note in its account book. It said that Mr. George Washington had been made an Entered Apprentice that evening. Washington was 20 years old. He paid a fee of two pounds and three shillings.

A *ledger* is a book where money and events are recorded. The lodge's ledger shows each step Washington took. He became a Fellow Craft on 3 March 1753 and a Master Mason on 4 August 1753. That is less than a year for all three degrees.
Washington stayed a Mason all his life. In 1788 he was named master of the lodge in Alexandria, Virginia, near his home at Mount Vernon. When he died in 1799, Masons took part in his funeral.
Some later stories made Washington the head of all American Masons. That is not true. No such office existed. The records show a real member, but not a national leader of the fraternity.

words.d: a book where money paid and received, and other events, are written down
the first degree, or step, of a new Mason

look.title: The Lodge Ledger, 1752
look.text: On 4 November 1752, the lodge treasurer writes that on this evening Mr. George Washington was made an Entered Apprentice, and records the fee he paid.
look.cite: Fredericksburg Lodge No. 4, ledger entry, 4 November 1752, as transcribed by the Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
look.prompt: Why is an account book written that same evening strong evidence that Washington joined?

check.q: Where did George Washington join a lodge in 1752?
check.why: The reading says a lodge in Fredericksburg, Virginia, recorded Washington joining on 4 November 1752.

check.q: What is a ledger?
choices: A book where money and events are recorded
check.why: The reading defines a ledger as a book where money and events are recorded.

lessons.title: Boston's Patriot Masons
lessons.mainIdea: Several Boston patriots, including Paul Revere and Joseph Warren, were active Masons.
reading: Paul Revere was a silversmith in Boston. He made cups, spoons and engraved prints. Today he is famous for his midnight ride in April 1775, warning that British troops were coming. He was also a devoted Mason.
Revere belonged to St. Andrew's Lodge in Boston. He stayed active for decades. In the 1790s he served as Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, the top leader of the state's Masons.

Another member was Dr. Joseph Warren, a Boston doctor and patriot leader. Warren led a group of Massachusetts Masons before the war. He was killed at the Battle of Bunker Hill in June 1775. John Hancock, who signed the Declaration of Independence first, was also a Mason.

So some well-known patriots were Masons. That is *documented*, which means proved by records from the time. But being in the same club does not prove the club planned the Revolution. Many patriots were not Masons, and many Masons were not patriots.

words.d: proved by records made at the time, such as ledgers, letters or minutes
in the American Revolution, a colonist who supported independence from Britain

look.title: Same Club, Same Plan?
look.text: Three players on a soccer team are also in the school band. The band wins a contest. A student says: the soccer team must have planned the band's win. Another student says: they are in both groups, but that does not show one group planned what the other did.
look.prompt: How is this like the claim that Masons planned the Revolution because some patriots were Masons?

check.q: What leadership role did Paul Revere hold in the 1790s?
choices: Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts
check.why: The reading says Revere served as Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts in the 1790s.

check.q: Which patriot Mason was killed at Bunker Hill in 1775?
check.why: The reading says Dr. Joseph Warren, a leader of Massachusetts Masons, was killed at Bunker Hill in June 1775.

check.q: Why does the reading say the club did not necessarily plan the Revolution?
choices: Many patriots were not Masons, and many Masons were not patriots

check.why: The reading says belonging to the same club does not prove a plan, since the groups only partly overlapped.

lessons.title: John Adams Says No
lessons.mainIdea: In 1798 John Adams wrote to Massachusetts Masons that he had never been made a Mason.
reading: In 1798, John Adams was President of the United States. The country was worried about a possible war with France. The Grand Lodge of Massachusetts sent him a friendly letter of support. Its Grand Master was Josiah Bartlett.

On 22 June 1798, Adams wrote back. He thanked the Masons warmly. Then he said something plain. He had never had the chance to be initiated into their fraternity. To be *initiated* means to be brought into a group through a ceremony.

Adams also praised the Masons he had known. He said many of his best friends were Masons. So the letter is friendly, not angry. It does not attack the lodge at all. It simply shows that he was not a member.
This is a strong kind of evidence. It is a *firsthand* statement, from the person himself, written at the time. Anyone who says Adams was a Mason has to explain away his own letter.

words.d: brought into a group through a special ceremony
coming directly from the person who saw or did something

look.title: Adams Writes to the Grand Lodge, 1798
look.text: Adams tells the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts that he has never had the honor of belonging to their ancient fraternity and has never been initiated. He adds that many of the friends he has valued most were Masons.
look.cite: John Adams to Josiah Bartlett and the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, 22 June 1798, Founders Online, National Archives (paraphrase)
look.prompt: What two things does Adams say in this letter? Why is it hard to argue that he was secretly a Mason?

check.q: What did John Adams tell the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts in 1798?
choices: He was their new Grand Master
He had never been initiated as a Mason
check.why: In his letter of 22 June 1798, Adams wrote that he had never been initiated into their fraternity.

check.q: What was the tone of Adams's letter?
choices: Friendly, praising Masons he had known
check.why: The reading says Adams thanked the Masons warmly and praised Masons he had known.

check.q: Why is Adams's letter a firsthand source?
choices: It was written by a historian in 1950
It was carved on a monument

check.why: Firsthand means coming directly from the person, and Adams wrote the letter himself in 1798.

lessons.title: Jefferson and the Missing Record
lessons.mainIdea: No record shows that Thomas Jefferson was a Mason, so careful historians say he is not known to have been one.
reading: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence. Later he became the third president. Many websites, posters and lists of famous Masons include his name. Is that true? Let's check the records.

Historians have looked for lodge records with his name. They have found none. Monticello, the museum at Jefferson's home, says he is not known to have belonged to any fraternal group such as the Freemasons. Even Masonic historians do not claim him as a proven member.

Notice the careful wording: "not known to have belonged." Historians rarely say "never" unless they have a statement like Adams's letter. With Jefferson, we have an *absence of evidence*, meaning no records turn up. That is different from proof that something never happened.

So the honest answer is this. We have no evidence that Jefferson was a Mason. Until someone finds a real record, a claim that he was one is *unsupported*. A lodge list, a letter or a minute could change that answer.

words.d: when no records or proof can be found for a claim
describes a claim that has no good evidence behind it

look.title: Three Ways to Say It
look.text: Statement 1: Jefferson was a Freemason. Statement 2: Jefferson was never a Freemason, and he said so. Statement 3: Jefferson is not known to have been a Freemason; no lodge record of him has been found.
look.prompt: Which statement best matches the evidence in this lesson? What is wrong with each of the other two?

choices: He was Grand Master of Virginia
He joined in Paris with Franklin

check.why: The reading says Monticello states he is not known to have belonged to any fraternal group such as the Freemasons.

check.q: How is the evidence about Jefferson different from the evidence about Adams?
choices: Jefferson wrote a letter saying he was a Mason
For Jefferson, no record is found; Adams wrote that he was not a Mason

check.why: Adams gave a firsthand statement, while for Jefferson there is only an absence of evidence.

choices: No records or proof can be found for a claim

check.why: The reading defines absence of evidence as no records turning up, which is different from proof that something never happened.

lessons.title: How Often Washington Went
lessons.mainIdea: In letters of 1798, Washington said he rarely attended a lodge and believed American lodges were not part of any plot.
reading: In 1798, many Americans were afraid of a secret group called the Illuminati. It had been started in Bavaria, in Germany, in 1776 and was shut down there in the 1780s. Books claimed it was secretly working through Masonic lodges.
A man named G. W. Snyder sent Washington one of these books. He worried that American lodges were in danger. Washington answered him in two letters, on 25 September and 24 October 1798.

Washington wrote that he did not lead any lodge. He said he had seldom been inside one in many years. He also said he did not believe any lodges in this country were spreading Illuminati ideas. He did think such ideas might be spreading in other ways.
These letters are useful. Washington was a real Mason, but in old age he said his part in lodge life had been small. Letters like these help us measure a claim, not just repeat it.

words.d: a secret society founded in Bavaria in 1776 and shut down in the 1780s
a statement that something is true, which may or may not have evidence

look.text: Washington tells Snyder that he presides over no lodge and has rarely been in one for many years. He adds that he does not believe any of the lodges in this country hold the ideas blamed on the Illuminati.
look.cite: George Washington to G. W. Snyder, 25 September 1798, George Washington Papers, Library of Congress (paraphrase)
look.prompt: What does this letter tell you about how active Washington was in his lodge late in life?

check.why: The reading says Snyder sent Washington a book claiming the Illuminati worked through lodges and worried about it.

lessons.title: The Capitol Cornerstone, 1793
lessons.mainIdea: On 18 September 1793, Washington helped lay the cornerstone of the U.S. Capitol in a public Masonic ceremony.
reading: A *cornerstone* is the first stone set at the corner of a new building. In the 1700s, laying it was a big public event. Masons often led these ceremonies. It made sense, since their fraternity took its symbols from builders.

On 18 September 1793, a crowd gathered on a hill in the new federal city, which would become Washington, D.C. The Grand Lodge of Maryland led the ceremony, with members of Alexandria Lodge No. 22 from Virginia. President Washington took part as a Mason.
Washington laid a silver plate with the stone. It recorded the date and the event. There was a parade, music and speeches. It was one of the most public things the Masons did in the young nation.
Here is a surprise. Today no one knows exactly where that cornerstone is. Searches have not found it. The ceremony is well documented, but the stone itself is hidden somewhere in the Capitol's walls.

words.d: the first stone set at a corner of a new building, often in a ceremony
a formal event done in a set way to mark something important

look.title: Washington's Masonic Life in Years
look.cite: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, Freemasonry; U.S. Senate, Washington Lays Capitol Cornerstone
look.prompt: How old was Washington, born in 1732, when he laid the Capitol cornerstone? How many years passed between joining and the cornerstone?

check.why: The reading says the ceremony took place on 18 September 1793.

check.q: Which Grand Lodge led the Capitol ceremony?
check.why: The reading says the Grand Lodge of Maryland led the ceremony, with Alexandria Lodge No. 22.

check.q: Why did Masons often lead cornerstone ceremonies?
choices: They owned all the land in the city
Their fraternity took its symbols from builders

check.why: The reading says it made sense for Masons to lead these events because their symbols came from builders.

lessons.title: Was the Revolution a Masonic Plan?
lessons.mainIdea: Masons fought on both sides of the Revolution, so the war cannot be called a Masonic plan.
reading: Some books and videos claim the American Revolution was planned inside Masonic lodges. It is a popular story, and it can sound convincing. Let's test that claim with what we know from the records.

First, Masons were on both sides. The British army had its own lodges that traveled with its regiments. Many British officers were Masons. In Boston, Prince Hall and fourteen other free Black men were made Masons in a lodge attached to a British regiment. Lodge histories give the date as 1775; a 2026 study argues for 1778.

Second, many key founders were not Masons. John Adams said so himself. Jefferson is not known to have joined. Careful counts of the 56 signers of the Declaration find proof of lodge membership for only a small number of them. Counts differ from source to source.

The claim is *unsupported*. Masons were part of colonial life, as churches and clubs were. Some patriots met in lodges. But no record shows the lodges as a body planning the war. Most Masons, like most colonists, simply took one side or the other.

words.d: describes a claim that has no good evidence behind it
a large unit of soldiers in an army

look.title: Sorting the Evidence
look.text: Fact 1: Paul Revere and Joseph Warren were patriot Masons. Fact 2: Many British officers were Masons in army lodges. Fact 3: John Adams said he was never a Mason. Fact 4: Only a small number of the 56 signers can be proved to be Masons.
look.prompt: Which facts might seem to support the claim of a Masonic plan? Which facts weaken it? What do you conclude?

check.q: What does the reading say about British army lodges?
choices: The British army banned all Masons
British lodges met only in London

check.why: The reading says the British army had lodges that traveled with its regiments, and many officers were Masons.

check.q: Where were Prince Hall and fourteen other free Black men made Masons?
choices: In the Grand Lodge of Maryland

check.why: The reading says they were made Masons in Boston in a lodge attached to a British regiment.

check.q: What is the best conclusion about the claim that Masons planned the Revolution?
choices: It is unsupported, because Masons were on both sides and many founders were not Masons
It is proved by the Capitol cornerstone

check.why: The reading shows Masons on both sides and many non-Mason founders, and no record of lodges planning the war.

lessons.title: A Seal for a New Nation
lessons.mainIdea: In 1776 the first Great Seal committee, with artist Pierre Du Simitière, proposed an eye in a triangle, but Congress did not adopt it.
reading: On 4 July 1776, the same day it approved the Declaration, Congress asked three men to design a seal. A *seal* is an official design stamped on important papers to show they are real. The three were Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and Thomas Jefferson.

They asked for help from Pierre Eugène Du Simitière, an artist living in Philadelphia. Franklin suggested a scene of Moses at the Red Sea. Jefferson suggested the people of Israel in the wilderness. The committee's final design mixed several ideas.

The committee's report of 20 August 1776 included an eye. It described the Eye of Providence in a glowing triangle, shining over the whole design. *Providence* means God's care and guidance. An eye like this was a common symbol of God's watchfulness in Christian art long before.

Congress set the design aside. But the eye idea stayed in the record. Of the three committee members, only Franklin was a Mason. Du Simitière has no records showing Masonic membership, so historians say he is not known to have been a Mason.

words.d: an official design stamped on important papers to show they are real
God's care and guidance over the world

look.title: The Committee's Report, 1776
look.text: The report describes the Eye of Providence inside a radiant triangle, with its glory reaching out over the shield and the figures of the design.
look.cite: Report of the first Great Seal committee, 20 August 1776, in Gaillard Hunt, The History of the Seal of the United States, Department of State, 1909 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: Where was the eye placed in this first design? Does the report say anything about Masons?

check.q: Who was on the first Great Seal committee in 1776?
check.why: The reading says Congress asked Franklin, Adams and Jefferson to design a seal on 4 July 1776.

check.q: What does Providence mean?
check.why: The reading defines Providence as God's care and guidance.

check.q: Which statement about Du Simitière fits the evidence?
choices: He was Grand Master of Pennsylvania
He is not known to have been a Mason
check.why: The reading says no records show Du Simitière as a Mason, so historians say he is not known to have been one.

lessons.title: The Pyramid Arrives, 1782
lessons.mainIdea: The pyramid under the eye was added in 1782, when Congress finally adopted the Great Seal.
reading: After the first design was set aside, Congress tried again. A second committee worked in 1780. A third worked in 1782. Each committee added ideas. None of them finished the job alone.

In June 1782, Charles Thomson, the secretary of Congress, took the best ideas from all three. A young Philadelphia lawyer, William Barton, helped with the back of the seal. Congress adopted the Great Seal on 20 June 1782.

The front shows the eagle. The back, called the *reverse*, shows an unfinished pyramid. At its base are the Roman numerals MDCCLXXVI, which mean 1776. Above it is the eye in a triangle. There are two Latin mottos. A *motto* is a short saying. One means that God has favored our undertakings. The other means a new order of the ages.

What did the unfinished pyramid mean? The designers explained it as strength and lasting power, with the country still being built. The eye showed Providence watching over it. The record shows no Masonic plan behind these choices.

words.d: the back side of a seal, coin or medal
a short saying that states a group's goal or belief

look.title: The Seal's Long Road
rows: State Department history of the seal
look.cite: Gaillard Hunt, The History of the Seal of the United States, 1909; National Archives, Great Seal of the United States
look.prompt: How many years passed between adopting the seal and putting it on the dollar? What does that gap tell you about who designed the eye?

check.q: When did Congress adopt the Great Seal?
check.why: The reading says Congress adopted the Great Seal on 20 June 1782.

check.q: What do the Roman numerals MDCCLXXVI at the base of the pyramid mean?

lessons.title: Onto the Dollar, 1935
lessons.mainIdea: The seal's eye and pyramid first went on the one-dollar bill in 1935, chosen by two men who were Masons.
reading: For more than 150 years, few Americans ever saw the back of the Great Seal. Then, in the 1930s, Henry A. Wallace read the State Department's history of the seal. Wallace was the Secretary of Agriculture. He took the idea to President Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Roosevelt liked it. In 1935, both sides of the Great Seal were printed on the back of the one-dollar bill. That is the design Maya was holding. It is still there today, on every one-dollar bill printed since.

Here is an interesting detail. Wallace and Roosevelt were both Masons. Years later, Wallace wrote that the eye had caught their attention because Masons also used an all-seeing eye as a symbol of God. So Masons did help choose to put the seal on the dollar.

But look closely at the *timeline*. The eye was proposed in 1776 and the pyramid adopted in 1782. Wallace and Roosevelt copied a design that already existed. They did not create it. Two different questions have two different answers.

lessons.title: Testing a Claim with the Paper Trail
lessons.mainIdea: A popular claim can be tested by asking who did it, when, and what records prove it.
reading: Let's go back to Maya's question: did the Freemasons put the eye on the pyramid? Historians test a claim by following the *paper trail*, the records made at the time, step by step.

Step one: who designed the eye? The 1776 committee and its artist, Du Simitière, who is not known to have been a Mason. Step two: who added the pyramid? Thomson and Barton in 1782. The records do not show a Masonic plan. Step three: who put it on the dollar? Wallace and Roosevelt in 1935, both Masons.

There is one more twist. Masons did use an all-seeing eye in their own art. It became common in American Masonic books by the late 1790s, after the seal was adopted. Historians still debate whether Masons used it earlier. Both the seal and the lodges drew on the older Christian symbol.

So the claim is partly true and partly false. Masons did not design the seal. Two Masons did choose to put it on the dollar. A good *conclusion* keeps both facts. It does not stretch one of them into a secret plot.

words.d: the records made at the time that show step by step what happened
a decision you reach after weighing the evidence
